_meta.purpose: STOF GraphQL Authorization Bypass Knowledge Base -- real disclosed bug bounty patterns for stof/modules/graphql_tests.py.
sources: PortSwigger Web Security Academy -- 'Bypassing GraphQL brute force protections' lab
PentesterLab / Wallarm Lab -- GraphQL Batching Attack writeups
_meta.key_finding: graphql_tests.py already covers field-level authorization bypass (TC-116.1) and object-level/BOLA mutation bypass (TC-116.2), both real and well-implemented. TC-116.3 (batched query bypasses a per-request auth check) was previously a stub, deliberately left NOT_IMPLEMENTED with the reasoning that it 'needs a specific rate-limited or step-gated mutation to meaningfully prove a batching bypass against -- too target-specific for a generic probe.' Dedicated research confirmed this reasoning was CORRECT for the field-probing shape TC-116.1 uses (aliasing a stateless per-field auth check has no reason to change its outcome), but INCOMPLETE: a genuinely generalizable construction exists by re-scoping TC-116.3 to the one rate-limited/step-gated flow every STOF-scanned target structurally has -- its own login endpoint's attempt limiter -- rather than an arbitrary business flow. This is exactly the documented real pattern (PortSwigger's own dedicated brute-force-bypass lab; Shopify HackerOne #481518): GraphQL aliases let a client request the same mutation N times under different names in ONE HTTP request, and most rate limiters count HTTP REQUESTS, not RESOLVED OPERATIONS -- so N aliased login attempts in one request can slip past a limiter that would have blocked the Nth of N sequential single-request attempts.

patterns.generalized_transformation: First establish a sequential baseline: send N single-operation login-mutation requests (one HTTP POST per attempt, wrong password each time) against the target's own GraphQL login mutation (if one exists) and record whether/at which attempt a rate-limit/lockout-shaped error appears. Then send the SAME N attempts as N GraphQL aliases inside ONE HTTP POST (`mutation { a: login(...) b: login(...) ... }`) and check whether the limiter still fires at the same point.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: The GraphQL endpoint's own login/authenticate mutation, if the schema exposes one (discovered via the same introspection TC-116.1/.2 already perform) -- NOT an arbitrary business-flow mutation, which is what made the original stub correctly judge a generic version unbuildable.
patterns.evidence_signal: A bypass is proven ONLY by a DIFFERENTIAL outcome, never by aliased-calls-returning-data alone (a normal successful call also returns data, so that alone proves nothing): (1) the sequential baseline must actually demonstrate the limiter firing at some attempt k (a rate-limit/lockout-shaped error appears) -- if the target has no lockout at all, there is nothing to bypass and the technique should report an inconclusive/PASS-with-caveat, not a FAIL: (2) the aliased single-request batch of the same N attempts must execute PAST attempt k without that same error appearing.
patterns.real_example: PortSwigger's dedicated 'Bypassing GraphQL brute force protections' lab (~100 aliased login mutations against a fixed username in one request); Shopify HackerOne #481518, a disclosed GraphQL rate-limit bypass via the same request-count-vs-operation-count mismatch.
patterns.operational_note: Unlike TC-116.1/.2 (single read-only or argument-validation-only probes), this technique deliberately sends multiple real wrong-password login attempts against the test account -- a real, if bounded and non-destructive (no valid credentials ever submitted), interaction with the target's own auth state. Must be gated behind allow_state_changing_probes like every other repeated-auth-attempt technique in this codebase, and bounded to a small N (a handful of attempts, not a real brute-force sweep) specifically to avoid actually locking out the test account for the rest of the scan.

stof_coverage.notes: graphql_tests.py's _technique_batching_bypass is no longer a NOT_IMPLEMENTED stub. It now runs live (async, given endpoint/session_manager/session_pool/evidence like TC-116.1/.2, moved into the same run_techniques() coroutine loop) whenever a GraphQL endpoint is found: gated behind GraphQLTestConfig.allow_state_changing_probes (SKIP if off, same convention as auth_tests.py's repeated-auth-attempt techniques), then finds a login/signin/authenticate-shaped mutation via _find_login_mutation() reusing the already-fetched introspection field names (SKIP if none exposed). If found, it sends GraphQLTestConfig.max_sequential_attempts (default 5) single-request wrong-password login attempts as a sequential baseline, watching for a lockout-shaped error via the new _looks_like_rate_limited() helper. A baseline that never locks reports PASS with an explicit 'inconclusive baseline' caveat (no limiter to bypass isn't a vulnerability) and does not proceed to the batch step. Only when the baseline demonstrably locks at attempt k does it send the same attempt count as ONE aliased-batch request (`mutation { a0: login(...) a1: login(...) ... }`); FAIL fires only on the genuine differential (baseline locked, batch did not), PASS fires if the batch still shows the same lockout-shaped error (limiter holds under aliasing). The top-level 'no GraphQL endpoint' SKIP branch in run_techniques() (this project's own demo.testfire.net target: REST-only, no GraphQL surface at all) still short-circuits TC-116.3 into a clean SKIP before any of this runs, unchanged from TC-116.1/.2's existing behavior -- confirmed live against demo.testfire.net (`stof test --module graphql_tests`), which correctly reports 'graphql_tests (no GraphQL endpoint discovered)' and never reaches the login-mutation-probing logic. The differential FAIL/PASS/inconclusive-PASS logic itself (baseline locking, aliased-batch bypass, aliased-batch limiter-holds) was validated only via unit tests against synthetic GraphQL schema/mutation fixtures in tests/unit/test_graphql_tests.py -- this project has no live target with a rate-limited GraphQL login mutation to observe the real differential against, so that path has not been observed live, only exercised via mocks.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Even where a target correctly enforces authorization at the flat, top-level field (TC-116.1) and top-level mutation (TC-116.2) layer, the same object frequently remains reachable -- with no authorization check at all -- by traversing to it through ONE level of a relationship/nested field on a DIFFERENT, permitted parent object (e.g. `user(id: "victim") { orders { id total } }`, or `order(id: X) { owner { email } }`). Resolvers for nested/relationship fields are commonly implemented as a raw data-layer fetch (e.g. `parent.getOrders()`) with no re-check of the caller's authorization against the child object, because the developer's authorization review focused on the top-level entry points.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: A query field discovered via the same introspection this module already performs (`_fetch_field_names`) that plausibly returns an object with sub-fields, probed by attempting a small, high-signal set of common nested sub-field names (id/email/total/amount/name) one level deep -- not by resolving the real GraphQL type system (STOF's introspection query here only asks for field names, not return types), the same black-box-hint philosophy TC-116.1's sensitive-field hint list already uses.
patterns.evidence_signal: Same evidence bar as TC-116.1, applied to the nested path specifically: a 200 response, no `errors` array, and a non-null value at `data.<field>.<subField>` returned to the low-privileged session. A GraphQL schema-validation error (selecting a sub-field name that doesn't exist on that type) is treated identically to an authorization-denial error -- both correctly fall through to the next candidate, since a black-box probe can't distinguish them and neither is evidence of a finding.
patterns.real_example: Documented as a distinct BOLA sub-pattern from flat field/object-level checks in the OWASP GraphQL Cheat Sheet and multiple disclosed GraphQL BOLA bug bounty writeups (Try Hack Me / HackerOne GraphQL BOLA reports): APIs that correctly gate `user(id)` and `order(id)` directly still leak the same data via `otherUser { orders { ... } }` or `order { owner { email } }` because the nested resolver never re-checks authorization against the traversed-to object.

stof_coverage.notes: graphql_tests.py's _technique_nested_relationship_bypass reuses _fetch_field_names (same introspection call TC-116.1/.2 already make) to enumerate candidate query fields, applies the same sensitive-field hint list TC-116.1 uses to prioritize candidates, then for each candidate field tries a small fixed set of nested sub-field hints (_NESTED_SUBFIELD_HINTS = id/email/total/amount/name) as a one-level-deep selection (`query { field { subField } }`). FAIL fires only on TC-116.1's exact evidence bar (200, no errors, non-null value) applied to the nested `data.<field>.<subField>` path; a schema-validation error from selecting a sub-field name that doesn't exist on the real type is treated the same as an auth-denial error (both fall through, matching _check_field_level_bypass_candidate's convention). Confirmed live against demo.testfire.net (`stof scan --module graphql_tests`), which reports SKIPPED via the module's own top-level 'no GraphQL endpoint discovered' branch -- this target has no GraphQL surface at all, so the live run never reaches the nested-probing logic. The differential logic itself (valid nested data returned vs. schema-validation error vs. auth-denial error) was validated via unit tests against synthetic GraphQL schema/nested-object fixtures in tests/unit/test_graphql_tests.py.

patterns.generalized_transformation: This module already sends a GraphQL introspection query (`{ __schema { queryType { fields { name } } mutationType { fields { name } } } }`) on every technique that needs to enumerate real field names to probe (TC-116.1, .2, .4), but previously discarded a successful, non-trivial result without ever turning it into its own finding -- even though GraphQL introspection left enabled on a production endpoint is itself one of the most commonly disclosed, real GraphQL misconfigurations (it is `TC-114` in this project's own `config/testcases.json`, and the OWASP GraphQL Cheat Sheet's first hardening recommendation). The fix is not a new query -- it's scoring the result this module already has.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: The same GraphQL endpoint every other TC-116.x technique targets, using the exact `_INTROSPECTION_QUERY` this module already sends internally via `_fetch_field_names` -- no new request shape.
patterns.evidence_signal: Deliberately honest, non-overclaiming framing per real disclosed-report practice: introspection succeeding and returning ANY non-trivial schema (at least one query or mutation field name) to a low-privileged/unauthenticated caller is reported as 'introspection is enabled' at Low/informational severity with an explicit note that this may be expected and acceptable on a non-production endpoint -- STOF has no reliable signal to distinguish production from development/staging for an arbitrary target, so the finding is framed as a fact for the pentester to triage, not an unconditional vulnerability claim. An empty schema (no query or mutation fields at all) is treated as introspection-disabled and reports PASS, not FAIL.
patterns.real_example: OWASP GraphQL Cheat Sheet's introspection-disclosure guidance; this project's own TC-114 (GraphQL Introspection Enabled, High severity in the general test-case catalog) documents the same underlying signal as a standalone, commonly-flagged finding in real GraphQL security assessments and bug bounty reports.

stof_coverage.notes: graphql_tests.py's _technique_introspection_exposed reuses _fetch_field_names (the exact introspection call TC-116.1/.2/.4 already make) and scores its own result: PASS (Low severity, not a finding) if both queryType and mutationType come back with zero fields (introspection appears disabled or errored), FAIL (Low severity, informational-toned Finding) if either returns at least one field name, with a description that explicitly notes introspection may be acceptable on non-production endpoints rather than asserting an unconditional vulnerability. Confirmed live against demo.testfire.net (`stof scan --module graphql_tests`), which reports SKIPPED via the module's own top-level 'no GraphQL endpoint discovered' branch, same as every other TC-116.x technique on this REST-only target -- the live run never reaches the introspection-scoring logic. The PASS/FAIL split itself was validated via unit tests against synthetic empty-schema and non-trivial-schema fixtures in tests/unit/test_graphql_tests.py.
